hero.title: Odor Predictor
hero.intro: What a molecule smells like depends largely on its structure. This project uses a graph neural network to predict, from the structure, the words flavorists would use for its smell, such as fruity, buttery or roasted.

method.title: How it works
flow.1.title: Molecule
flow.2.title: Graph
flow.2.sub: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges
flow.3.title: Graph neural network
flow.3.sub: atoms pass information to their neighbors, 3 rounds
flow.4.title: Odor descriptors
flow.4.sub: a probability for each of 138 words
method.data: Data. 4,886 molecules with expert odor descriptions from two flavor and fragrance databases (The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell), merged and cleaned by the OpenPOM project. Each molecule has about 5 of 138 possible descriptors.
method.model: Model. Each atom starts with a few simple properties: element, number of neighbors and hydrogens, charge, aromaticity and whether it is in a ring. In each round every atom collects information from the atoms bonded to it. The result is pooled into one summary of the whole molecule and turned into 138 probabilities. The model has about 140,000 parameters, small enough to run in a web browser.
method.eval: Data split. Molecules with rings were split into training (80%), validation (10%) and test (10%) sets by ring scaffold, so the test set contains ring systems the model never saw. This is harder than a random split.
method.explain: Atom contributions. The coloring on the tool page uses occlusion: each atom is removed in turn, the model is run again, and the change in the descriptor's probability is recorded. Atoms whose removal lowers the probability (orange) are what the model relies on; atoms whose removal raises it (blue) hold the prediction down. This shows which structures the model weighs, not that they chemically determine the odor.
results.intro: Performance is measured with AUROC. Take one molecule that has a descriptor and one that does not: AUROC is the chance that the model gives the first one a higher score. 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect. The numbers below are averaged over all 138 descriptors on the 488 test molecules.
results.seed_note: Graph neural network: scores of the model deployed on this page. Across 3 training runs with different random seeds, the overall score was {mean} (standard deviation {std}). The baselines describe each molecule by a list of the small structural fragments it contains (a Morgan fingerprint) and use standard machine learning methods.
results.takeaway: The graph neural network beats both conventional baselines by about 0.02 AUROC. The gain is modest but consistent across random seeds and across most descriptors. Molecules with ring systems not seen during training are clearly harder (about 0.80).
results.label_note: Only descriptors with at least 10 positive molecules in the test set are listed.
ablation.intro: Two ideas from PharmaGNN (Liu et al., J Sci Food Agric 106, 8114-8120, 2026, doi:10.1002/jsfa.70826) were tested: an asymmetric loss (ASL) that puts more weight on rare descriptors, and three pharmacophore flags per atom (hydrogen-bond donor, hydrogen-bond acceptor, hydrophobic group; RDKit's standard definitions, which the browser can reproduce exactly). The paper's 3D charge and logP descriptors cannot be computed identically in the browser and were not used. Each of the four setups was trained 3 times on the same scaffold split:
ablation.note: Test AUROC: mean ± standard deviation over 3 training runs. Rare descriptors: mean AUROC over the third of descriptors with the fewest positive training molecules ({n}).
ablation.takeaway: The differences between the four setups are within run-to-run noise, and rare descriptors got slightly worse, so this page keeps the original model. Possible reasons: the paper used a random split, while this site uses a harder scaffold split; the pharmacophore flags overlap with the existing element and hydrogen-count features; and the paper's model architecture differs. The asymmetric loss also inflates output probabilities about fourfold, which is unsuitable for display.
limits.title: Limitations
limits.4: Predictions for ring systems unlike anything in the training data are noticeably weaker (AUROC about 0.80).
limits.6: Not for safety decisions. It says nothing about toxicity, allergenicity or regulatory status.
footer.data: Data and acknowledgements: the model was trained on data from The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell & Associates (Sanchez-Lengeling et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.10685, CC BY-NC), curated and merged by OpenPOM (Barsainyan et al., 2023); the raw data and odor labels are not redistributed here. The model and its predictions are for non-commercial academic demonstration only.
footer.thr: Odor thresholds: L.J. van Gemert, Odour Thresholds: Compilations of Odour Threshold Values in Air, Water and Other Media, 2nd ed., Oliemans Punter & Partners, 2011. Representative values are taken where available from Czerny et al., Eur. Food Res. Technol. 228, 265-273 (2008), as listed there.
footer.ref: Related work: Lee et al., A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception, Science 381, 999-1006 (2023). doi:10.1126/science.ade4401; Liu et al., PharmaGNN: a model for odor prediction based on graph neural networks, J Sci Food Agric 106, 8114-8120 (2026). doi:10.1002/jsfa.70826
footer.fi: Used in: Flavor Improver (as the single-molecule odor source).
